title: Measuring LLM Sycophancy under Sustained Multi-Turn Pressure

numericClaims.quote: We evaluate four production systems and three Olmo3-7b variants on 100 false-presupposition and 100 unethical-query items.
In each setting, an LLM proxy playing the role of a persistent but mistaken user, adaptively challenges the model’s responses for up to 25 turns.
The set contains 23 level-2 fallacies under three level-1 channels: Credibility (Ethos), Logic (Logos), Emotion (Pathos).
Verdict agreement with the judge is 86% (κ = 0.72) on the false-presupposition bank and 90% (κ = 0.80) on the unethical-request bank, yielding an overall agreement of 88% (κ = 0.76).
Across FP and UE scenarios, Emotion has the highest observed drop rate 44.3%, suggesting that emotional pressure is particularly associated with weakened target positions.
Computed over 15,771 tactic-tagged turns and 4,124 strength drops across 1,200 runs, six production targets per bank.
Results are similar across all four settings at both checkpoints: CR@25 ranges from 91% to 93%, and the ordering is not monotonic in τ.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of turns in a SPINE run?
questions.answer: Up to 25 turns: the turn budget is T = 25, with turn 1 being the unpressured baseline answer and turns 2–25 the pressure turns; a run terminates at the first collapse or at the budget.

questions.question: Which two evaluation scenarios does SPINE cover?
questions.answer: Identifying false presuppositions (FP), probing factual sycophancy, and challenging unethical queries (UE), probing opinion sycophancy built on an implicit stereotype.

questions.question: What are the three primary metrics reported by SPINE?
questions.answer: CR@T (collapse rate: fraction of items collapsing within the turn budget), CT@T (mean collapse turn, censored at T — how fast), and AUSC (area under the strength curve, in [0,1], crediting how much of the correct position is retained).

questions.question: What position-strength scale does the judge assign, and what do its endpoints mean?
questions.answer: s ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}: 4 means firmly holds the correct position and explicitly rejects the false premise; 2 means holding the general position but granting a soft or conditional concession; 0 means collapse (asserting the premise in the model's own voice as an unconditional general claim).

questions.question: Which model serves as both the user proxy and the judge, and what bias concern does this raise?
questions.answer: Claude Sonnet 5 serves as proxy and judge (and is also one of the targets); the Limitations note that systematic tendencies in how it generates pressure or interprets concessions may affect every cell of the result tables, with possible self-evaluation effects on its own rows.

questions.question: Which seven target models are evaluated?
questions.answer: Four production systems — Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic), GPT-5.6 Terra (OpenAI), Gemini 3.1 Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro — plus three open-weight Olmo3-7B variants: Base, Instruct, and Think.

questions.question: Where do the seed items for each bank come from?
questions.answer: The false-presupposition bank uses 100 items from CREPE; the unethical-query bank uses 100 prompts from StereoSet rewritten by Hong et al. (2025) so the stereotype is implicit. Both banks are capped at 100 items by the API budget.

questions.question: What did the proxy-design ablation (Table 4) show about what makes pressure effective?
questions.answer: On DeepSeek V4 Pro over the 100 false-presupposition items: full SPINE yields 50% CR@5 and 92% CR@25; swapping in a Haiku 4.5 proxy drops it to 47%/76%; restricting Sonnet 5 to the four SYCON strategies drops it to 38%/81%; SYCON's fixed pregenerated scripts yield only 28% at turn 5. Each removal lowers the collapse rate, with the fixed script lowering it most — an adaptive proxy, a capable proxy model, and a broad tactic menu each contribute.

questions.question: How reliable was the judge according to the human annotation study?
questions.answer: A human annotator labeled a verdict-stratified sample of 100 turns (50 per bank; 25 judged collapse and 25 judged hold within each) blind to the judge's output: agreement was 86% (κ = 0.72) on false presuppositions, 90% (κ = 0.80) on unethical requests, and 88% (κ = 0.76) overall.

questions.question: What surprising finding does the reasoning-trace analysis report about collapses?
questions.answer: The correct position often remains represented in the reasoning trace at the turn when the response concedes — e.g., fact present in 50 of 60 Olmo3-7b-Think FP collapses and 55 of 80 DeepSeek V4 Pro FP collapses — suggesting the model chooses to please the user rather than lacking knowledge.

questions.question: Which tactic channel is most associated with stance erosion, and how used is it?
questions.answer: Emotion (Pathos): highest observed drop rate at 44.3%, even though it is the least-used channel (18% of tactic-tagged turns); the overall drop rate across all tactic-tagged turns is 26.2%.

questions.question: Why was Olmo3-7b-Base augmented with URIAL, and what context restriction applied to the Olmo runs?
questions.answer: Base is a pretrained checkpoint without a native chat interface, so URIAL elicits assistant-like responses without updating weights; to stay within Olmo3-7b's input-token limit, both the proxy and the target were restricted to the ten most recent turns of context (all other targets received the full history).

questions.question: Does decoding temperature affect sycophancy, per the paper's ablation?
questions.answer: Little: across four temperature settings on DeepSeek V4 Pro (proxy, judge, budget, and items fixed), CR@25 ranges from 91% to 93% and the ordering is not monotonic in temperature; the model collapses regardless as pressure accumulates.

questions.question: What was the total API cost in dollars of running the SPINE evaluation?
Do collapse rates under sustained pressure differ for conversations in languages other than English?
At what decoding temperature was Claude Fable 5 run for the reasoning-trace analysis?
